nodes.label: Letter of inquiry
nodes.one_line: Write a one-to-three-page LOI that gets a foundation to invite your full proposal instead of passing.
know_what: the one-to-three-page LOI format most foundations expect before a full proposal
the difference between a letter LOI and a form-based inquiry in foundation portals
what a program officer screens for: fit, feasibility, and a competent ask
the five standard sections: hook, problem, approach, outcomes, and the ask itself
the convention that attachments and appendices are not invited unless stated
know_how: read the foundation's LOI guidelines and mirror its section order and page limit exactly
open with the problem in one paragraph with named evidence, not your organization's history
state the approach in concrete terms a reviewer can picture, naming methods and partners
put the ask in numbers and years early enough that it cannot be missed
close with a specific next step: invite the full proposal, or a call
check the portal deadline and submission mechanics before writing a word
habits: researching the funder before drafting, never after
keeping a reusable LOI boilerplate bank of problem, approach, and outcomes paragraphs
treating the LOI as the first screening, not a warm-up for the real proposal
recording every foundation's LOI deadline and format in the pipeline tracker
re-reading the funder's stated priorities immediately before the final pass to catch drift
nodes.checkpoint: Draft an LOI in a foundation's stated format, under its page limit, that a colleague reading it cold can restate the ask, the problem, and the approach — and send it to a foundation whose priorities you can name.
nodes.common_failure: Writing the LOI before researching the funder, so it reads as boilerplate; treating it as a miniature full proposal until it is too dense to screen; burying the dollar ask; missing a portal deadline because the format was assumed, not checked.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Jane Geever, The Foundation Center's Guide to Proposal Writing

nodes.label: Review-criteria mapping
nodes.one_line: Walk your finished draft against the funder's published scoring criteria and confirm each one is answered with evidence, not implication.
know_what: published review criteria: the scoring rubric reviewers actually fill in
the difference between answering a criterion with evidence and with implication
how scoring weights change where effort should go in the draft
federal scoring conventions such as the NIH 9-point scale versus foundation pass/fail rubrics
the fact that page limits and criteria both come from the same NOFO or guidelines document
know_how: extract every criterion and its weight from the NOFO or foundation guidelines before revising
build a criteria-to-section map: each criterion named, the section that answers it, the evidence cited
walk the finished draft section by section, tagging each criterion answered, partial, or unanswered
rewrite every partial and unanswered tag with named evidence, not stronger adjectives
recheck the map after each revision pass so a rewrite cannot orphan an earlier answer
give the map to a second reader whose only job is to find an unanswered criterion
habits: reading the criteria before drafting, never after the deadline
keeping the criteria map open beside the draft while writing
checking every factual claim in the draft carries a named source
treating 'it answers that criterion by implication' as a warning sign
re-extracting the criteria if the funder issues a revised NOFO or guidelines mid-draft

know_why.claim: Mapping the draft to the funder's published criteria is the surest way to make reviewers see every answer they are paid to score.
know_why.because: reviewers score against a rubric under time pressure and skim for evidence; an answer they cannot find scores as absent.
know_why.disputed_by: some program officers warn that criteria-mirroring reads as gaming the review and that authentic fit outscores checklist alignment.
know_why.source: practitioner debate in The Grantsmanship Center Magazine and program-officer commentary at grantee conferences

nodes.checkpoint: Produce a criteria map for a real draft with every published criterion tagged answered, partial, or unanswered, and close every partial and unanswered tag before submission.
nodes.common_failure: Mapping after the deadline; mistaking implication for evidence; reconstructing criteria from memory instead of reading the actual NOFO; ignoring scoring weights and spending the pages on an unweighted section.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Revision loop
nodes.one_line: Run a structured read-through with a critical reader and revise against criteria and page limits until the draft is submittable.
know_what: the difference between editing sentences and revising the argument
structured read-through: reading the draft as the reviewer, not the author
what a critical reader can catch that the author cannot: assumptions, gaps, buried asks
page-limit trimming techniques: cut boilerplate, merge sections, move content to attachments
version control for drafts so no revision is lost or reverted by accident
know_how: run a structured read-through: read once for argument, once for criteria, once for limits
recruit a critical reader with specific questions, never a blank 'does this look good?'
revise against the criteria map, closing every unanswered tag before touching prose
trim to page limits by cutting whole sections of boilerplate before cutting evidence
re-run the criteria map after each pass and freeze the version when it passes
submit the frozen version, not the latest edit
habits: never submitting a first draft, ever
reading the draft aloud or printed to break the author's glaze
tracking each revision against a named criterion or limit
treating 'it's fine' as incomplete feedback and asking for one specific problem
keeping a revision log with the frozen submittable version clearly marked
nodes.checkpoint: Submit a proposal that has passed at least one structured read-through by a critical reader, with every review-criteria item confirmed answered and the draft within every page limit.
nodes.common_failure: Polishing instead of revising — fixing sentences while the argument is wrong; revision by committee until the voice dies; ignoring page limits until the final hour; one editing pass with no criteria check, then submitting a draft that scores zero on an unanswered criterion.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Carlson & O'Neal-McElrath, Winning Grants Step by Step
Beverly Browning, Grant Writing For Dummies
